Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.

MAHA's midterm report card
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides, saying he has used some of them himself.

item.title: Trump administration wants to remove regulations on a super planet-heating gas
item.description:
Climate
Trump administration wants to remove regulations on a super planet-heating gas
October 28, 20265:15 PM ET
By
Julia Simon
,
Kirk Siegler
Flares burn off methane and other hydrocarbons at an oil and gas facility in Lenorah, Texas, Oct. 15, 2021.
David Goldman/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
David Goldman/AP
The Trump administration is proposing to dramatically scale back a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut methane emissions from the oil and gas industry at drilling sites nationwide.
Methane is a major contributor to climate change and is estimated to be 80 times more planet-warming than carbon dioxide in a twenty-year time frame. In 2023, the Biden administration finalized rules that were meant to rein in methane emissions from the oil and gas sector.
President Trump made the announcement while campaigning in Lubbock, Texas, Tuesday, saying his administration's revision, under the Clean Air Act, would save the industry billions in production costs and spur more domestic drilling. The proposal comes as Republicans face a backlash from voters over high gas prices heading into the midterms.

item.title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
item.description:
Work
Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
October 28, 202612:10 PM ET
By
The Associated Press
Dolores Huerta is seen at the California Democratic Party's 2025 State Convention at the Anaheim Convention Center in Anaheim, May 31, 2025.
Court Mast/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Court Mast/AP
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.

item.title: What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
item.description:
What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
October 28, 20269:05 AM ET
By
Kat McGowan
Cookie Jones, left, quit her job to provide care to her mother who has Alzheimer's disease. Caregivers often earn less as they take time off work to help aging family members.
Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.

item.title: Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
item.description:
Europe
Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
Updated October 28, 20266:35 PM ET
Originally published October 28, 20266:09 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday.
Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
